entities.name: The Black Book of Communism
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Black Book of Communism, published in 1997, is a seminal work that chronicles the repressive regimes and atrocities committed under communist governments throughout the 20th century. Authored by a group of scholars including Stéphane Courtois, this text covers the global impact of communism, detailing the deaths of approximately 100 million people across various countries, including the Soviet Union, China, and Cambodia. It matters in historical discourse as it challenges the perception of communism as a benign ideology, instead framing it within the context of systemic violence and oppression.

The text draws on extensive archival research and firsthand accounts to document the policies and actions of key figures such as Joseph Stalin, Mao Zedong, and Pol Pot. The authors meticulously catalog events such as the Great Leap Forward in China (1958-1962), which resulted in the deaths of an estimated 15-45 million people, and the Khmer Rouge's genocide in Cambodia (1975-1979), where approximately 1.7 million were killed. Through its detailed analysis, The Black Book of Communism not only presents historical facts but also argues for the moral and ethical implications of communism, affecting the way historians and the public perceive political ideologies.

The legacy of The Black Book of Communism extends beyond its initial publication, as it has influenced scholarly debates surrounding totalitarianism and human rights. It has become a cornerstone in the study of 20th-century history, prompting discussions about the accountability of political regimes. The impact of this work is evident in its reception, leading to further research and literature on the consequences of communist rule, as well as shaping public opinion and policy toward communist states in the post-Cold War era.
